1:
Gill traces the relapse to the peace itself: it was the fruit of long rest, as often happens with a people favoured with plenty, who abuse their mercies and forget the giver — the principal evil, unnamed, being idolatry. Henry says the same and presses it into three observations. There is the strange strength of corruption, which hurries men into sin despite the most frequent experience of its fatal consequences, the bent to backslide being restrained only with great difficulty. There are the common ill effects of a long peace: eighty years of rest should have confirmed them in their religion and instead made them secure and wanton, for the prosperity of fools destroys them, and Jeshurun waxeth fat and kicketh. And there is the loss a people sustains when good governors die — the verse may be read that they did evil because Ehud was dead, since he had kept a strict eye on them, and when he was gone they revolted, having feared him more than they feared God. Clarke asks a sharper question: why when Ehud was dead, and not when Shamgar was dead? Does that not intimate that Shamgar was never reckoned among the judges?

Ellicott takes Jabin for a dynastic name — it means he is wise, and may have served as Pharaoh and Abimelech and Agag did — and Clarke supposes this king a descendant of the Jabin whom Joshua defeated, who had gathered the wrecks of that army. Both are answering a real difficulty, which Ellicott states at length. The resemblance between the two defeats is strange: in both a Jabin king of Hazor, in both subordinate kings, in both chariots prominent, and even some of the same names among the conquered. He offers two ways out. If the received chronology stands, then in the century and a half since Joshua's death Hazor rose again from its ashes under a new settlement whose king took the old dynastic name; if instead the whole period of the Judges must be shortened, the armies of Joshua and Barak may have attacked from different directions in one campaign, each tribal record preserving only the part its own people fought in. He will not pretend either is free of difficulty, and closes on the principle: we must remember the antiquity and the fragmentary nature of the records, which were written with other and far higher views than furnishing us an elaborate consecutive history. Keil holds that the song of the next chapter is a commentary on the event rather than the quarry it was dug from, since the prose carries details we look for in the song in vain.

Henry counts three things that made this servitude worse than the ones before. The enemy was nearer than any former oppressor, within their borders and their bowels; he was a native of the country, bearing an implacable enmity for the invasion that had dispossessed him, and the more cruel when he had them in his power for the sake of the old quarrel; and these Canaanites had once been conquered by Israel, sentenced of old to be their servants, and might have been under their feet still had not Israel's own slothfulness and unbelief let them get head — so that to be oppressed by those their fathers had conquered and they themselves had foolishly spared could not but be very grievous. What lay behind it he states in a sentence: they alienated themselves from God as if he were none of theirs, and then God alienated them as none of his, for those who threw themselves out of his service threw themselves out of his protection. Clarke explains the nine hundred chariots as armed with iron scythes — not made of iron throughout, but shod with it, or fitted with blades projecting from the axle by which infantry could be cut down.
4:
Her name means bee, as Gill, Henry and Ellicott all note, answering the Greek Melissa; Henry says she answered it in her industry and sagacity and her great usefulness to the public, her sweetness to her friends and her sharpness to her enemies, and Ellicott quotes Cornelius à Lapide for the same thought more compactly, that she had a sting for foes and honey for friends. Whether Lapidoth was a man is less settled. Gill takes it for her husband's name and dismisses the Jewish notion that the husband was Barak himself on the strength of a likeness in the names, Barak meaning lightning and Lapidoth lamps; Clarke says the original may as well be rendered a woman of Lapidoth as the wife of Lapidoth. Ellicott prefers the wife, noting that the phrase closely resembles Huldah the prophetess, wife of Shallum. Both he and Henry pass on Rashi's alternative, that she was called a woman of lamps from making the wicks for the lamps of the sanctuary — Henry adding that having stooped to that mean office for God she was afterwards thus preferred.

What she was is more remarkable than what she was called. Ellicott states it plainly: she is the only female judge, indeed the only female ruler of any kind in Jewish history apart from Athaliah, and the only judge to whom the title prophet is expressly given — a title implying poetic as well as prophetic gifts, and justified in her by her predictions, her lofty courage and the splendour of her song. He looks abroad for parallels, to the Teutonic prophetesses Veleda and Alaurinia and to Joan of Arc, and marks the difference: among the Jews prophetesses were the exception, among the ancient Germans they were the rule. Clarke calls it the first instance of female government on record, observing that Deborah seems to have been supreme in civil and religious affairs alike while Lapidoth appears to have had no hand in the government. Henry defines the office more narrowly. She judged not as a princess, by civil authority conferred upon her, but as a prophetess and as God's mouth to the people, correcting abuses and redressing grievances, especially such as concerned the worship of God — so that men came to her less for the deciding of controversies between neighbours than for advice in reforming what was amiss in things pertaining to God. Keil, who takes her seat under the palm as the securing of her people's rights at home, marks that she summoned Barak in order to secure those rights against their foes abroad also. Henry adds a shrewd guess about how she was tolerated at all: perhaps, being a woman, she was the more easily permitted by the oppressor to do it.

The palm is the detail everyone lingers on. Henry allows either that she had her house beneath it, a mean habitation that would couch under a tree, or that she had her judgment-seat in the open air under its shadow — an emblem, he thinks, of the justice she administered there, which thrives and grows against opposition as palms do under pressure. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew says she was sitting rather than dwelling, which may mean only that she took her station under that solitary and well-known tree when giving judgment, as Abraham lived under the oak of Mamre and Saul under the pomegranate of Migron. He also draws out Dean Stanley's contrast, between the triumphant mother of Israel under her palm, full of the fire of faith, and Judaea Capta on the coins of Titus, a weeping woman seated under a palm tree with downcast eyes and folded hands and extinguished hopes. And he marks what the seat implies about the woman: unlike the German Veleda, who lived in a tower in awful seclusion, Deborah allowed the freest access to her presence.
6:
Gill notes that in sending for Barak, Deborah acted not as a private person but as a judge in Israel, exercising public power and authority — and that the summons itself tells against the Jewish notion that Barak was her husband, since a wife and husband would have lived together. Ellicott finds the man's quality in the same fact: Kedesh lay in the far north, and that his fame had reached the southern limits of Ephraim shows he must have been a man of great mark. His name means lightning, as does Barca, the family name of Hannibal and Hasdrubal; Virgil calls the Scipios two lightnings of war. Clarke reads the appointment as further evidence of Deborah's standing, since to name the general of the armies is the act of one who possesses the supreme power in the state. On the word rendered draw, Ellicott is candid that the meaning is uncertain, the versions dividing between depart, lead and spread out, but takes it probably to mean that Barak was to gather his troops in small contingents, so as to prevent suspicion.

The two places named are the battle. Clarke gives Maundrell's Tabor: a mountain standing by itself two or three furlongs within the plain of Esdraelon, with a fertile oval area at the top, one furlong broad and two long, and a prospect reaching to the Mediterranean; very difficult of ascent, an hour's climb, which with the grand area at the summit made it a proper place for the rendezvous of Barak's army. Ellicott says the same more briefly — the broad flat top of a strong and easily fortified hill would serve the double purpose of watch-post and stronghold, its truncated cone of limestone rising isolated from the plain some nineteen hundred feet. Of the Kishon he observes that the word is nachal, not a river but a torrent-bed, the Arabic wady; it is always named in connection with this victory because the overthrow of Canaan was due in great measure to the providential swelling of the torrent-waters, which turned its banks into a morass and rendered the iron chariots worse than useless. It is now called the Mukatta, the river of slaughter. Maundrell had guessed as much, that the stars fighting against Sisera means the rains that made the Kishon high and rapid enough to sweep the host away as it tried to ford.

Barak's condition divides the commentators. Keil denies that it sprang from distrust of the promise: his mistrust was of his own strength, and what he wanted was the divine enthusiasm which the prophetess's presence would infuse into him and into the army gathering round him. Ellicott, noting how daring and hopeless the enterprise looked, allows that much was gained for the army by her presence, but calls the Septuagint's addition — because I know not the day in which the Lord prospers the angel with me — a sort of excuse for his want of perfect faith. Clarke reads the same addition the other way. Barak was certain of his call but not of its timing, and wished the woman on whom the Spirit constantly rested to tell him when to strike the blow he knew would be decisive; that is quite natural and quite reasonable, and no impeachment whatever of his faith. She goes, and the prize goes elsewhere. Ellicott renders the sentence thy pre-eminence shall not be on the path which thou enterest, and reminds us of the humble and almost down-trodden position of women in the East, so that a great warrior could hardly fail to feel the humiliation. Clarke asks whether the woman is Deborah claiming the conquest or a prediction of Jael, and thinks Jael the likelier; Ellicott agrees, for Barak may have supposed it was the prophetess, but it was the wife of the nomad chief.
10:
Gill supposes the muster was raised either by the sound of a trumpet, as Ehud raised his, or by messengers sent to the two tribes; Ellicott observes that the verb is the technical one for summoning an army, and that in the first instance it will have been only the leaders who were invited to a conference, like those of the Swiss on the Rütli in 1307. What the ten thousand were is disputed. Clarke says flatly that they were footmen, since Barak had no chariots and his army was composed wholly of infantry, and Henry thinks the phrase may intimate as much, the disproportion of strength against horses and chariots being thereby made very great and the victory the more illustrious. Ellicott will not have the idiom carry that weight: at his feet means simply after him, as the same book elsewhere renders it. Henry gets his own good out of the words either way. God is said to call us to his feet, that is, into obedience to him; and the men at Barak's feet were cheerful and ready to follow him whithersoever he went.

Ellicott notices which tribes answered and why. Zebulun and Naphtali would be harder to arouse than the central tribes, for though they felt the oppression most they would also have to bear the brunt of the vengeance in case of defeat, whereas Ephraim and Benjamin, stronger and more secure, could raise their contingents without the prophetess coming in person. Henry reads the song of the next chapter back into the muster and finds that some came in from Manasseh and Issachar, and that more were expected from Reuben, Dan and Asher who never came; the narrative here overlooks them all, and tells us only that to make the ten thousand effective indeed Deborah went up with him. Her presence, and God's, was abundantly sufficient to balance the disproportion in chariots. Ellicott adds that a trace of her going may survive in the name Debarieh, a village at the foot of Tabor.

Henry explains why Heber is introduced just here, in the middle of a muster: the removal of this one Kenite family out of the wilderness of Judah in the south into the northern country is set down for the sake of what is to follow about Jael. Gill calls Heber a descendant of Kain and a principal man among the Midianites, whom the Targum names the Salmaean. Ellicott corrects two things in the verse. The Hebrew says not that Heber was of the children of Hobab but that he had separated himself from them, nomadic settlements being constantly liable to send off such colonies; and Hobab is Moses' brother-in-law rather than his father-in-law, the words for these relationships lying close together. He also thinks the plain of Zaanaim wrong: the word is elon, which our translators constantly render plain because they were misled by the Targums and the Vulgate, though they render the cognate allon oak. It should be the terebinth in Zaanaim — a tree worth naming, since the terebinths on the hills of Naphtali were fine enough to give the tribe its emblem, Naphtali is a branching terebinth. Zaanaim itself means wanderings, or the unlading of tents, which suits a nomad settlement; and Ellicott sets against it the promise that Jerusalem shall be a tent that wanders not.
12:
Who carried the news to Sisera is left open. Gill will allow either some of the Canaanites living near Tabor or spies Sisera kept out, and mentions that some fasten it on the Kenites, who were at peace with Jabin, though whether they told him out of good will or ill will cannot be said; what is certain is that God's providence so ordered it that by one means or another he should be informed. Ellicott thinks the guess unnecessary. The verse about Heber was brought in by way of anticipation, so that a reader who last heard of the Kenites in the south of Judah should not be surprised to meet them in Naphtali a few verses on; the they may simply be impersonal, as the Greek and Latin have it, it was told. Sisera's answer to the report is measured. Ellicott reads it as the judgment of a soldier who saw at once that this very sudden revolt had assumed formidable proportions, and that he would need all his forces to dislodge Barak from so strong a position; Gill accounts for the gathering by supposing the chariots had been quartered in different places.

Clarke sees the point of Deborah's presence discharged in a single word. This, he says, is exactly what Barak wanted her for: he did not know the day, and she told him the precise time — up, for this is the day. Ellicott sets the same clause against the practice of the age, which attached the utmost importance to fortunate and unfortunate days, and marks the difference: Barak was guided by a prophetess and not by idle auguries. Gill is careful with the word up, which cannot mean go higher, since they were already on the top of a mountain; it means bestir thyself, put the army in rank and file, and march to meet the enemy without delay. Ellicott measures what obedience cost. Having neither cavalry nor chariots, it required no little faith in Barak to abandon his strong post and take the aggressive against the kind of force that struck most terror into Israelites.

The verb rendered discomfited is the hinge of the battle, and all four take it the same way. Keil observes that it is the word of Exodus and Joshua, denoting the confounding of a hostile army by a miracle of God, and mostly by some miraculous phenomenon of nature — which puts Sisera's overthrow in the same category as Pharaoh's. Clarke describes the result: chariots breaking and overthrowing chariots, universal disorder in every rank, so that Barak and his men had little to do but kill and pursue. What the phenomenon was, Gill and Ellicott both answer out of Josephus, that as the ranks closed a violent storm of rain and hail came on and the wind drove it into the faces of the Canaanites, so that their slings and arrows were useless and their armoured men too benumbed to hold a sword, while the storm at Israel's back did them less harm — a tradition Ellicott judges sound, since the song of the next chapter speaks of the swollen Kishon and the storm. Gill also passes on Abarbanel's account of a noise in the heavens like a great army, with horses and chariots of fire. Ellicott explains why the general came down from his chariot rather than fleeing in it: he had far more chance of concealment on foot than in the well-known chariot of a commander, and the vehicle was in any case probably struggling in the trampled morass. Of the pursuit to Harosheth he notes only that a rout in which the fugitives must cross a river and fight a storm is always specially fatal, and that the memory of this carnage survived for years, together with the circumstance that the soil was enriched by the dead.
17:
Henry follows the steps of the fall. The chariot had been Sisera's pride and his confidence, and we may suppose he had despised the armies of the living God for having neither chariot nor horse; justly then is he made ashamed of it and forced to quit it. Then, with no strong-hold of his own in reach, he flees to a way of living he had probably ridiculed, and the more because religion was kept up among the Kenites. Ellicott notes that he ran in the opposite direction from his army, which made for Harosheth, and arrived a starving and ruined fugitive. He chose a woman's tent for the reason Clarke gives out of Eastern etiquette: no man intrudes into the women's apartment, and such tents were held inviolably secure, so he might lie there unsuspected till the pursuit went by. Henry adds what emboldened him: there was no league between Jabin and Heber, only an absence of hostility, Jabin having never troubled so quiet and harmless a people.

Gill and Henry both picture Jael at the tent door, waiting for news of a battle fought near enough for her to know it was expected. What she meant by going out to meet him is the question. Henry allows that in seeming to relieve his fatigue she may really have intended to retard his flight until Barak came up, but doubts whether she had at first any thought of taking his life — that, he thinks, God afterwards put into her heart. Ellicott finds the going out itself decisive: it makes it probable that her design was already formed, unless a chieftainess stood above the ordinary rules that govern Oriental women; and since nothing is said of Heber, he may have been absent, or have kept out of the way to further his wife's purpose. Without that special invitation, he adds, Sisera would never have ventured to violate every law of propriety by entering the privileged sanctuary of the harem, and her fear not was no idle word, treachery being far too common among Bedouin tribes for the reassurance to be needless. Keil sees nothing but the usual form of oriental hospitality — she turned him aside from the road, and covered him with a rug that he might sleep, being thoroughly exhausted with his flight.

Ellicott suspects the request for water. It was natural enough in itself, but he had not made it on arriving, and to taste food in the tent was a way of binding the inviolable laws of hospitality still faster. Clarke observes that she gave more than was asked, and that this kindness increased his confidence and security. What she gave has been argued over. Keil holds she handed him milk from her skin simply to give her guest a friendly reception, and dismisses as worthless later decoration both Josephus's claim that the milk had already turned and R. Tanchum's that it intoxicated a weary man. Ellicott is willing to grant the first and not the second: soured milk is likely enough, buttermilk being a common drink in Arab tents, but Tanchum's intoxication and Rashi's deep sleep, with the object of stupefying him, are giving reins to the imagination. On the lie he is asked to tell, Clarke explains why it would have worked — no man would intrude, so the bare words there is no man in my tent would preclude all search. Henry marks that she made no such promise, and draws the rule: we must not sin against God, no, not to oblige those we would show ourselves most observant of. Ellicott answers that it is very unfair to judge ignorant nomads and idolatrous Canaanites of that age by the standard of Christianity, when a lie in such straits was thought perfectly natural, and the heathen advice of Darius stood — when it is necessary to lie, lie.
21:
Gill accounts for the weapon by the household: there were no arms in the tent, for the Kenites used none, so she took up the iron pin by which the tent was fastened to the ground. Clarke and Ellicott agree it was one of the great pegs that hold down the cords, though Josephus calls it iron and the Greek a wooden plug, and nothing in the text decides. The hammer he would render the hammer — the ponderous wooden mallet kept in every tent for beating down those pegs, whose name makkebeth gave the Maccabees their title. She went softly, so as not to wake him, and Clarke explains why one blow sufficed: he lay on his side, overwhelmed with sleep through the heat and fatigue of the day, and the piercing of the temples must in a moment have put him past resistance. Ellicott takes the clause about his being fast asleep and weary to be there only to account for his not waking at her approach and her preparations — unless it carries a passing touch of pity.

What the writer thinks of the deed is the question the chapter leaves hardest. Gill supplies an inward warrant: it was now put into her heart to kill him, an impulse upon her spirit which the effect it had on her persuaded her was of God, since it filled her not with malice and revenge but with concern for the glory of God, the interest of religion and the good of Israel. Ellicott rejects that reading in the strongest terms he uses anywhere in the chapter. Many have ventured to assume that at this instant Jael received a divine intimation of what she was to do; but to make such an assumption as a way of defending an act of assassination peculiarly terrible and peculiarly treacherous seems to him unwarrantable to the last degree, and those who adopt such methods for themselves ought not to press these private interpretations upon others. A mind unsophisticated by the casuistry of exegesis, he says, will reach a fair estimate of her conduct without interpolating suppositions into the narrative. Keil grants more of the premise and still refuses the conclusion. Deborah's word was fulfilled to the letter, the Lord having sold Sisera into the hand of a woman and taken the glory of the victory from Barak; but neither that prophecy nor the praise given her in the song of the next chapter makes the act itself morally justified, even allowing that she acted under the influence of religious enthusiasm.

Ellicott also answers the argument from the narrative's silence. The description is exceedingly graphic, and no word of censure is attached to its worst and darkest features; but that by no means excludes the most complete disapproval, since the method here is the method of all ancient literature and wholly unlike the modern habit of subjective reflection — Homer will relate an atrocity without a word of comment, and elsewhere indicate what he thinks of it by a single casual adjective. He wonders too whether the needless words Heber's wife are emphatic, recalling the peace between Jabin and the house of Heber that was mentioned when the name last occurred, though he thinks it more likely to be the inartificial manner of a very ancient record. Then Barak comes up, and Keil observes that she went out to meet him to show him what she had done. Clarke will not guess what the sight cost the victor: what impression it made is not said, but it could not have given him much pleasure, especially when he learned the circumstances of the death. Ellicott ends on the tableau — the undaunted murderess standing in her tent between the dead chieftain and the living one, glorying in the decision that had flung to the winds every rule of Eastern morality and decorum.
23:
How quickly Jabin fell is not agreed. Gill reports from Josephus that as Barak went towards Hazor he met the king, slew him and destroyed the city; but Gill thinks what follows in the text points the other way, to a total conquest accomplished afterwards and gradually. Keil reads the Hebrew so: the hand of Israel went on becoming heavier and heavier in its pressure upon him until they had destroyed him and he warns that the overthrow of Jabin and his rule did not involve the extermination of the Canaanites generally. Clarke gives the phrase the same literal turn, going went and was hard, and takes it to mean that Israel followed up the victory until the kingdom as well as the king was destroyed.

Clarke will not close the chapter without putting Jael's act on trial, and he draws the indictment himself in ten counts. There was peace between her family and the king of Canaan, made as such treaties always were with a sacrifice and an oath. Knowing this, Sisera came to her tent with the utmost confidence, and she met him with friendly greetings and assurances of safety. She hid him in the secret part of her own tent and undertook to deny his presence to any who inquired. Having given him shelter and refreshment she was bound by the rules of Asiatic hospitality to defend his life at the hazard of her own; instead she took the advantage of his weariness and deep sleep and took his life, then met Barak and showed him in triumph what she had done. Do we not find here, he asks, bad faith, deceit, deep hypocrisy, lying, breach of treaty, breach of the laws of hospitality, deliberate and unprovoked murder? The one defence ever offered is that she was sincere at first and afterwards divinely directed; that would vindicate her, for God may dispose of the lives of his creatures as he pleases, but there is no sufficient evidence of any such direction. Jael says nothing of her motives, and the sacred penman says nothing either, but states the fact as he stated Ehud's and leaves the reader to form his own opinion. Clarke will not have the plea that a public enemy may be killed by any of the people he oppresses, calling it a very dangerous position that refers a solemn act of justice to the caprice of any man who persuades himself he is authorised. His own verdict is a refusal of verdict: I will not justify, I dare not absolutely condemn; there I leave them.

Ellicott answers the argument that the verse itself settles the matter. That the deliverance is here credited to God — and to Elohim, where the rest of the narrative says Jehovah, an interchange whose law he does not pretend to have formulated — does not involve the least approval of the false and cruel elements that stained Jael's courage and faith. God overrules even criminal acts to the fulfilment of his purposes, while the crimes themselves meet their own condemnation; the case of Jehu is decisive, whose conduct was likewise of a mixed character, an instrument in God's hand against the house of Ahab, dauntless and believing, and yet justly condemned by the prophet for his atrocious cruelty. To read this clause and Deborah's cry, so let all thine enemies perish, as making the work of Jael the work of God is to claim divine sanction for wishing that hostile powers should always so perish, by cruel and treacherous assassination. Yet he refuses the opposite excess as well. Jael is not to be classed with women moved only by a demoniacal thirst for vengeance, like Criemhild in the Nibelungenlied, but with those, like Judith of old and Charlotte Corday in modern times, who took themselves for the champions of a great and good cause.
